dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Next.js/Vite contract from vendored source

evidence.note: Read both next-shims.d.ts files, grounding some API signatures (useRouter, getStaticProps, etc.) in the vendored contract — a genuine contract-reading step.
Read fixture apps thoroughly (pages, configs, middleware, instrumentation, SSR pages) and a couple of test specs to scope the contract before coding.
Sustained across the entire build: repeatedly grep/read individual e2e .spec.ts files as an executable spec to learn expected behavior before each fix — a strong, self-correcting investigation trait.

All /opt/reference access is merely ls/cp of node_modules for dependency resolution; the agent never opens next-source, vite-source, or plugin-rsc source. grep confirms next-source=0, vite-source=0, plugin-rsc=0.
Explicitly works 'from memory' of Next.js APIs; RSC/hydration and Vite plugin-hook behavior are figured out by guessing and experiment rather than reading upstream implementation.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reads the next-shims.d.ts contracts (anchor 5 trait) and — notably — uses fixture apps and test spec files as an executable spec throughout the whole build (an anchor-8 trait), which lifts it well above the level-3 'skims one or two files' description. However, the defining behavior of this dimension — reverse-engineering mechanics from the vendored next-source/vite-source/plugin-rsc trees — is entirely absent: those source trees are never opened, the Vite plugin API and RSC/hydration are handled from prior knowledge and empirical trial. This mixed profile (grounded shim signatures + heavy test/fixture cross-checking, but no upstream source mining) sits between anchors 3 and 5, landing at 4.

dimensions.name: Structuring the build across subsystems and routers

evidence.note: Up front reads filter.json categories, both fixture apps, and e2e specs to size the scope and enumerate subsystems (RSC, ISR, server actions, middleware, routers), establishing the feature landscape before building.

Explicitly sequences foundational pieces first: package skeleton -> CLI (dev/build/start) -> plugin/module resolution -> 'focus on pages router with SSR first since that's the simpler case, then expand' — dependency-ordered, simplest-first sequencing.

After pages router reaches ~50/74 passing, treats app router as 'the next big chunk (~250 tests would benefit)' and lays out a numbered sub-plan (discover routes, layouts, dynamic, route handlers, error/not-found). Done-signal is a concrete fixture-test subset count.

Re-prioritizes by failure category value ('unlock ~30 tests'), targeting app-router hydration and next-compat hooks; runs narrowed per-fixture playwright subsets (e2e/pages-router/hydration) as milestone checks.

Throughout the long build, tracks pass-count progression (31->160->176->216->276->302/325) and repeatedly picks the next milestone by 'look at remaining and prioritize' — the plan is used to decide what to build next, though it lives in ad-hoc prose rather than a maintained explicit milestone artifact (no TodoWrite; many 'Plan: wait.' filler).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly identifies the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible dependency order — CLI/plugin/resolution and pages-router SSR before app router, then dependent features like hooks/ISR/caching — with concrete done-signals per milestone (specific fixture rendering and per-subset test pass counts), matching the level-8 anchor. It also re-prioritizes adaptively by which failure category unlocks the most tests, a level-10 trait. However, the sequencing is emergent prose embedded in analysis rather than a maintained, explicit layered milestone plan, so it falls short of 8/10's fully explicit tracking; a 7 best captures strong dependency-ordered, test-tied, adaptive sequencing without a persistent structured plan.

dimensions.name: Using and extending the test suite as a correctness oracle

evidence.note: Symlinks vinext into pages-basic, boots `vinext dev` in background, and curls specific routes (/, /about, /api/hello, /old-about) to verify page render, API routes, and redirects as narrow per-subsystem probes rather than relying only on the suite.
Parses /tmp/playwright-env-results.json with Python to isolate failures by category (pages-router vs app-router) and prioritize fixes — well beyond a coarse pass/fail gauge.
Runs a targeted single spec (`npx playwright test e2e/pages-router/hydration.spec.ts`), but this is the ONLY targeted-subset playwright run; the dominant loop otherwise re-runs the full 335 suite.
Detects a regression (302→250) after an error-boundary change and reverts, treating the stable 302/325 as a checkpoint — genuine self-correcting verification.

Aware of the 335→373 range but forms no strategy to generalize beyond visible tests or guard against overfitting; verification does not separately target build/start paths in isolation (all manual boots use `vinext dev`).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent far exceeds anchor 5: it not only runs run_tests.sh regularly and spot-checks fixtures, but builds real narrower probes (manual app boots + per-route curls) and isolates failures by parsing the results JSON per category, catching regressions and using green counts as checkpoints. It falls short of a full 8 because targeted test-subset runs were used only once, the post-bootstrap loop leaned on the slow full suite rather than consistently tight per-subsystem loops, and it never verifies dev vs build vs start paths in isolation. It shows none of anchor 10's generalization/anti-overfit design despite knowing about the hidden 373 superset. This places it at a 7, between anchors 5 and 8.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-count and remaining scope across a long build

evidence.note: First full run: '31/325 passing! Most failures are app-router tests since I haven't implemented app router' — establishes baseline and maps the bulk of failures to a subsystem.
Sustained delta-tracking across runs: '160/325 (was 31)', '201/325 (was 176)', '216/325 (was 201)', '227/325 (was 222)', '238/325 (was 227)' — a continuously updated pass-count picture.

Detected regression immediately ('Down to 199! That regressed'), attributed it to specific subsystems (nested dynamic routes, route priority, navigation flows), and tracked recovery '233 (was 238 then 199 then 233)'.

Caught two large regressions from client-side error/loading boundaries ('Big regression to 246', 'Big regression to 250') by comparing against best-known count and reverted each time; but re-attempted the same error-boundary approach twice, a minor circular thrash.
Recognized diminishing returns near the end — skipped 'heavy' SSE streaming, pursued 'quick wins', settled at 302/325 as stable, and distinguished raw 306-passed from 302 filter-matched.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent systematically monitored pass-count deltas across ~30 test runs, attributed failures to specific named subsystems, and caught regressions immediately by comparing against the prior known-good count, reverting each time — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because it briefly circled on the client-side error boundary (regressing twice with a similar change) and some subsystem attribution was approximate rather than a precise done-vs-remaining map, so it does not fully meet the 'reliably recognizes thrashing before wasting effort' bar.

dimensions.name: Revising approach as the contract and constraints emerge

evidence.note: Diagnosed React/index.js CJS loading failure under ssrLoadModule and revised the resolution strategy to Node import() with CJS interop — an early architectural correction driven by observed failure.

Persistent React module-instance mismatch (Vite deps_ssr cache vs react/cjs). Re-derived the actual mechanism from Vite's dedupe/optimizeDeps behavior, tried multiple resolutions, and confirmed the hooks page worked before running full tests.

Reconsidered hydration target (body vs html vs document) and switched to renderToReadableStream when renderToString couldn't handle async server components — deliberate subsystem redesign against upstream reality.
Iterated through Suspense/React.use wrapping and promise caching for async-component hydration, each time checking pass-count and adjusting when console-error fixtures regressed.
Detected pass-count regressions (238->199; 302->250) caused by its own changes and reverted, treating drops as signals rather than barrelling ahead.
Recognized CJS user-code interop and interactive error boundaries needed deeper rework but chose to skip/revert rather than re-derive — a boundary that keeps this below the 10 anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly treated surprising failures (React instance mismatch, async-component hydration, HMR port collisions) as signals to re-examine assumptions, deliberately redesigned resolution/rendering strategies, and confirmed new approaches against the test suite before proceeding — squarely the level-8 behavior. It caught its own regressions (drops to 199 and 250) and backed them out, but corrections occasionally regressed other subsystems requiring reverts, and a few falsified areas (CJS interop, interactive error boundaries) were abandoned rather than re-derived, keeping it short of the continuous, non-regressing reconciliation described at 10.

rubric.task_read: The agent must build 'vinext' — a from-scratch Vite-based reimplementation of a large Next.js feature surface (dual routers, SSR, SSG, server actions, middleware, caching, a next/* interception plugin, CLI, CJS support) into a single package, using only vendored reference source and no next dependency. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-complexity build with an under-specified contract that must be reverse-engineered from vendored source and fixture shim files, and a concrete 335→373-test acceptance oracle. It demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep reference-reading, layered decomposition across many subsystems, disciplined use of the test suite as a verification loop, and continual course-correction as the API contract is discovered.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Next.js/Vite contract from vendored source
dimensions.description: Reading the vendored next/vite source, fixture next-shims.d.ts contracts, and test fixtures to infer exact API signatures and behavior before/while implementing each subsystem.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The contract is implicit: no docs, no internet, and correctness is defined by upstream behavior and the shim type signatures. Guessing signatures for useRouter, getStaticProps, after(), or the Vite plugin hooks leads to silent, compounding failure across dozens of tests.

anchors.0: Starts coding vinext from memory of Next.js APIs without opening the vendored source or shim files.
anchors.3: Skims one or two files (e.g. a shim) but largely relies on prior knowledge; misses how Vite plugin hooks or RSC actually resolve modules.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant next-shims.d.ts contracts and the key vite plugin API before implementing each major subsystem, grounding signatures in the vendored types.
anchors.8: Systematically mines both the npm dist trees and the next-source TypeScript for the mechanics of each subsystem (routing, SSR, caching, server actions), cross-checks against fixture apps and the test files to learn expected behavior, and records the discovered contract.
anchors.10: Sustains targeted, hypothesis-driven investigation across the whole build — repeatedly returning to upstream source to resolve specific behavioral ambiguities as they surface, tracing how vite@8/plugin-rsc implement resolution and hydration, and using fixtures/tests as an executable spec so nearly every implementation choice is evidence-backed rather than guessed.

dimensions.name: Structuring the build across subsystems and routers
dimensions.description: Breaking vinext into an ordered hierarchy of buildable, independently checkable subsystems (CLI, plugin/module resolution, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, server actions, hooks) with clear done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The feature list spans many interdependent systems; without sequencing (e.g. plugin/resolution and basic SSR before SSG and caching) the agent cannot get any tests green and risks a giant unverifiable lump of half-working code.

anchors.0: No breakdown; attempts to write the whole package in one undifferentiated push.
anchors.3: A flat, vague list ('add routing', 'add SSR') with no ordering by dependency and no per-item completion check.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible dependency order, with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, dependency-ordered milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete done-signal (a specific fixture app rendering, or a test subset passing) and foundational pieces (plugin, resolution, dev server) are sequenced before dependent features.
anchors.10: Plan is layered and adaptive: milestones are sized to yield frequent verifiable wins, tied to specific slices of the test suite, re-sequenced as dependencies are discovered, and used throughout to decide what to build next rather than authored once and abandoned.

dimensions.name: Using and extending the test suite as a correctness oracle
dimensions.description: Deliberately driving progress with run_tests.sh and per-fixture checks, plus building narrower probes (single app boot, single route render) rather than assuming subsystems work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 335-test suite is the given oracle, but it is slow and coarse; the agent must design tighter feedback loops per subsystem and anticipate the hidden 373-test superset, verifying behavior not just the visible tests.

anchors.0: Never runs the tests or any app; declares subsystems done by inspection.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail gauge but has no finer-grained verification and doesn't isolate failures.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh regularly and uses failures to guide fixes, plus some manual spot-checks of fixture apps.
anchors.8: Builds tight per-subsystem verification loops (booting individual fixture apps, targeting test subsets, checking dev vs build vs start paths separately) and treats each green milestone as a checkpoint before moving on.
anchors.10: Designs a layered verification strategy that generalizes beyond the visible 335 tests — probing edge behaviors implied by the contract, guarding against overfitting to specific tests, and confirming correctness across dev/build/start and both routers so that the hidden superset is likely to pass too.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-count and remaining scope across a long build
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which subsystems/tests pass, what remains, and detecting when a fix is regressing others or when effort is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to lose the plot, chase one failing test while breaking five, or thrash on a subsystem without noticing lack of progress.

anchors.0: No awareness of overall pass/fail trajectory; works feature-to-feature with no sense of remaining scope.
anchors.3: Occasionally notes a pass count but doesn't track regressions or map failures to subsystems.
anchors.5: Keeps a running sense of pass-count and what's left, and notices when a change breaks previously passing tests.
anchors.8: Systematically monitors pass-count deltas across runs, attributes failures to specific subsystems, and detects stuck/circular states (re-debugging the same area) early enough to change tack.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, continuously-updated map of done-vs-remaining across all subsystems, catches regressions immediately by comparing against a known-good baseline, and reliably recognizes thrashing or diminishing returns and redirects effort before wasting a long stretch.

dimensions.name: Revising approach as the contract and constraints emerge
dimensions.description: Changing architecture, resolution strategy, or subsystem design when reality (test failures, upstream behavior, Vite plugin limits) contradicts an initial assumption.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reimplementing Next.js on Vite involves many assumptions that will prove wrong (how RSC/actions resolve, how caching interacts with SSR, CJS interop); barrelling ahead on a falsified design wastes enormous effort on this horizon.

anchors.0: Sticks to the first design regardless of failures; repeats the same failing approach.
anchors.3: Makes local patches to symptoms but won't revisit a flawed architectural choice even when evidence mounts.
anchors.5: Adjusts approach when a subsystem clearly won't work, backing out a wrong design after reasonable evidence.
anchors.8: Treats surprising failures as signals to re-examine assumptions, revises the design or resolution strategy deliberately, and confirms the new approach against the tests before proceeding.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles design with discovered reality — promptly abandoning falsified approaches, re-deriving the correct mechanism from upstream source, and propagating the correction across affected subsystems without regressing others, sustaining forward progress despite repeated contract surprises.
